headline: 8,150 handshakes on New Year's Day
summary: Roosevelt opens 1907 by meeting sociologist Edward A. Ross, then comes down to trumpets for the New Year's reception: diplomats first, then the public, 8,150 hands in all, a record that stood for decades. Afterward he washes up, takes the family for a country drive and goes to Bamie's N Street house for chocolate, whipped cream and champagne. He ends the day reading Gissing on Dickens and Lowes Dickinson's The Greek View of Life.

headline: Naval personnel bill with Foss
summary: Roosevelt discusses the naval personnel bill with Representative Foss and receives a string of senators and congressmen. He writes California's Governor Gillett about the Japanese question.

events.detail: Visitors include Beveridge, Allison, Elkins and Longworth

letters.topic: The Japanese question

headline: San Francisco backs down; nature fakers
summary: Roosevelt presses Root and Governor Gillett to block California bills excluding Japanese children, and later wires San Francisco's mayor congratulations when the school order is withdrawn. Chaco Canyon becomes a national monument, J. P. Morgan briefs him on shaky markets, and he tells John Burroughs he has finally sailed into Long, Jack London and the other nature fakers.

events.detail: Urges Root to stop California's anti-Japanese school bills
Immigration with Sargent, Straus and Bonaparte
Los Angeles water supply with Flint
The financial situation with J. P. Morgan
Postal appointments with Hemenway and Beveridge
Gives an interview attacking nature fakers

letters.topic: Stop California's school exclusion bills at any cost
Head off anti-Japanese laws in California
Telegram: congratulations on rescinding the school order
Thanks for his help on the Japanese issue
An article about the government
Two letters about leasing coal land
Morgan wants him to meet railroad men to calm the markets
He has publicly taken on the nature fakers

tr_quotes.text: You will be pleased to know that I finally proved unable to contain myself, and gave an interview or statement, to a very good fellow, in which I sailed into Long and Jack London and one or two other of the more preposterous writers of 'unnatural' history.

uncertain: This entry appears to merge three days' records (March 10-12) under one date. The record also notes the government's $70 million deposit of customs receipts in New York banks.

headline: Enforcing the eight-hour day
summary: Roosevelt talks with Taft about enforcing the eight-hour law and talks immigration with Beveridge, Lodge, Dixon and Flint. Lacey and Gamble also call.

events.detail: Immigration with Beveridge, Lodge, Dixon and Flint

headline: Inland Waterways Commission; panic on Wall Street
summary: Roosevelt creates the Inland Waterways Commission, chaired by Theodore Burton, to study the nation's rivers for power, flood control and reclamation; its members include Pinchot, Newell, W J McGee and Senator Newlands. The same day panic hits the New York Stock Exchange. He talks federal railroad control with A. B. Stickney and sends Burton the commission's charge.

events.detail: Panic selling hits the stock exchange in New York
Federal railroad regulation with A. B. Stickney

letters.topic: The new coins
Japanese school segregation
Instructions for the Inland Waterways Commission

headline: Cabinet confronts the market panic
summary: The Cabinet meets on the Wall Street panic, and Roosevelt confers with Cortelyou about it. He also sits down with mine union chief John Mitchell and the mine owners, and asks the Interstate Commerce Commission to value every railroad as a basis for fair rates.

events.detail: Cabinet on the Wall Street panic
Meets Mitchell and the mine owners

letters.topic: How the railroads and the administration get along
Value each railroad to set its proper rates

headline: Harriman and the Illinois Central
summary: Roosevelt meets James Speyer and several senators on the financial situation, and Illinois Governor Deneen and his attorney general, Stead, about Harriman and the Illinois railroad. He writes Secretary Wilson on labeling blended whiskey.

events.detail: Finances with Heyburn, Crane, Beveridge and Speyer
Harriman and the Illinois railroad with Deneen and Stead

letters.topic: How blended whiskeys should be labeled
Honor Taft's wishes on Ohio appointments

headline: Waterways appointments made public
summary: The names on the Inland Waterways Commission are published. Cousin Emlen Roosevelt calls that evening.

headline: Opening an exposition by telegraph
summary: At 3:30 Roosevelt presses a button that opens the Louisville exposition. He discusses South Dakota patronage with Gamble and tells Thomas Page he is less and less willing to talk with railroad men.

events.detail: Opens the Louisville exposition by pressing a button

letters.topic: His growing reluctance to meet railroad men

headline: Railroads with C. S. Mellen
summary: Roosevelt confers on politics with Hansbrough and on railroads with New Haven president Charles S. Mellen, and meets Franklin K. Lane. He thanks Ernest Pollard and the other congressmen who backed the ship subsidy bill.

events.detail: Visitors: Bacon, Garfield, Jusserand, Heyburn and Hitchcock

letters.topic: Thanks for supporting ship subsidies

headline: A crowded lunch table with Bryce
summary: Roosevelt hosts a large lunch that includes Ambassador Bryce and much of the Cabinet. He confers with Taft and Major Scott about West Street buildings, and with Hitchcock and Ballinger.

events.detail: Large lunch with Bryce, Root, Taft, Cortelyou, Garfield, Bonaparte and others
West Street buildings with Major Scott and Taft

headline: A visitor from Groton
summary: Roosevelt confers with Senator Overman and receives Jusserand, Root and George Marvin of Groton School.

headline: Waterways commission meets the President
summary: Roosevelt meets the new waterways commission and its chairman, Burton and lunches with Jusserand, Meyer and Brooks Adams. He asks Richard Bowker to report on conditions in Panama in light of Stevens's complaints and departure.

events.detail: Meets the Inland Waterways Commission with Burton
Lunch with Adams, Meyer, Jusserand and others

letters.topic: A report on Panama after Stevens's charges and resignation

headline: Tobacco trust and new coins
summary: Roosevelt takes up Indian matters with Garfield and Leupp, the tobacco trust with F. H. Levy, the canal commission with Joseph Blackburn, and the new coinage with Roberts. He writes Illinois Attorney General Stead, who is probing Harriman's railroad stock transfers.

events.detail: Indian affairs with Leupp and Garfield
The tobacco trust with F. H. Levy

letters.topic: His inquiry into Harriman's stock dealings

headline: Speck von Sternberg on Sunday
summary: Ambassador Speck von Sternberg calls at 2:30.

headline: Bat Masterson drops by
summary: Roosevelt and Beveridge discuss making New Mexico and Arizona states, and frontier lawman Bat Masterson is among the callers. Roosevelt tells Taft he opposes printing complete government records of every American war, and tells Jacob Schiff that Wall Street sees him as a wild-eyed revolutionary.

events.detail: Admitting New Mexico and Arizona, with Beveridge
Visitors include Bat Masterson, Ben Daniels and Fairbanks

letters.topic: Against publishing full records of the nation's wars
How Wall Street views him
Harriman's charges against the ICC

uncertain: 'Del. Andrews' read as New Mexico's territorial delegate William H. Andrews.

headline: Henry Adams sees him hesitate
summary: Henry Adams writes that everyone, even the President, is tired, and that Roosevelt seems unsure for once about the financial strain. Roosevelt meets Cortelyou, Root, Lane and Clark on railroads, lunches at Dr. Rixey's, and holds an immigration meeting with members of the new commission.

events.detail: Railroads with Clark, Lane, Root and Cortelyou
Immigration with Burnett, Latimer, Lodge, Dillingham, Jenks and Neill
State appointments with Scott and Dalzell

headline: Carnegie to lunch; another dental visit
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Andrew Carnegie, two Navy captains and several officials, meets the Interstate Commerce Commission, and goes to the dentist.

events.detail: Lunch with Captains Lee and Simpson, McCormick, Bacon, Cortelyou, Fairbanks and Carnegie

headline: Toothache, boils and an unbending course
summary: Roosevelt's tooth aches, Ted is suffering from boils, and Archie is still mending. He writes Jacob Schiff about Wall Street's view of him and tells Henry Higginson, amid the market turmoil, that he will not budge from his chosen path.

events.detail: Ted has boils; Archie still recovering

letters.topic: Wall Street's opinion of him
Finances and railroad manipulation; he will hold his course

tr_quotes.text: I will not deviate one hand's breadth from the course I have marked out.

headline: More railroad talks
summary: After the Cabinet, Roosevelt meets Neill, Knapp and Cullom on railroads. Wisconsin's Governor Davidson and James W. Gerard are among the callers.

events.detail: Railroads with Cullom, Knapp and Neill
Visitors: Cortelyou, Brownlow, Governor Davidson, Gerard and Meyer

headline: Down over Brownsville
summary: Roosevelt confers on the canal with Representative Marshall and on railroads with August Belmont, J. M. Levy and Frank Kellogg. He praises Ray Stannard Baker's article on the Atlanta riot and race, admitting the Brownsville affair has left him depressed.

events.detail: Railroads with Kellogg, Levy and Belmont

letters.topic: Praise for his Atlanta riot article; low spirits over Brownsville

tr_quotes.text: I have been really deprest over this Brownsville

uncertain: Levy's initials are unclear in the record and are read as J. M.

headline: Easter: everyone mending
summary: On a cold, rainy Easter, Roosevelt writes Kermit that Archie has recovered, Quentin is fine and, in his father's words, 'as quaint and funny as ever,' and Ted has spent the past three days ill. He adds that he dislikes seeming to speak only to move the stock market.

events.detail: Writes Kermit with news of his brothers' health

letters.topic: Easter weather, the boys' health, and the stock market

tr_quotes.text: and as quaint and funny as ever
I do not like to seem to talk just for the effect upon the Stock Market.
